c-7.4-forecasting-tcpi.title: 7.4 Control Costs (continued): EAC forecasting methods, ETC, VAC, reserve analysis, TCPI, Table 7-1
c-7.4-forecasting-tcpi.notes: Figure 7-12: cumulative S-curves of PV, EV and AC against a data date, with BAC, EAC, ETC, management reserve and project budget marked - example over budget and behind schedule. Forecasting: when BAC is no longer viable, consider the forecasted EAC; forecasts are projections from current performance and other knowledge, regenerated from work performance data. EAC is typically actual cost for completed work plus an estimate to complete (ETC). Most common: the PM and team's manual bottom-up forecast - EAC = AC + bottom-up ETC (new estimate of the remaining work), compared with calculated EACs for risk scenarios using cumulative CPI and SPI. Three common calculated methods: (1) ETC at the budgeted rate - EAC = AC + (BAC - EV): accepts actual performance to date but assumes future work at plan; when performance is unfavourable, assume improvement only if supported by risk analysis; (2) ETC at the present CPI - EAC = BAC / CPI: past cost efficiency continues; (3) ETC considering both SPI and CPI - EAC = AC + [(BAC - EV) / (CPI x SPI)]: useful when the schedule affects remaining effort; variants weight CPI and SPI (80/20, 50/50). Reserve analysis during control: monitor contingency and management reserves - still needed, used for risk responses, add savings from captured opportunities to contingency or take as margin/profit, remove unused contingency when risks don't occur, request more if new risk analysis requires. TCPI: the cost performance that must be achieved on the remaining work to meet a management goal = cost to finish outstanding work / remaining budget. TCPI based on BAC = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC); once an EAC is approved it may replace BAC: TCPI based on EAC = (BAC - EV) / (EAC - AC). Figure 7-13: if cumulative CPI falls below baseline, remaining work must immediately be performed at TCPI (BAC) to stay within the BAC; whether achievable is a judgment (risk, time remaining, technical performance); the alternative is the TCPI (EAC) line. Table 7-1 (verified): PV - authorised budget assigned to scheduled work; EV - work performed in terms of its authorised budget (EV = sum of PV of completed work); AC - realised cost of work performed; BAC - sum of all budgets for the work (the cost baseline); CV = EV - AC (positive under cost, neutral on, negative over); SV = EV - PV (positive ahead, neutral on, negative behind); VAC = BAC - EAC (positive under, negative over); CPI = EV / AC (>1 under cost, 1 on, <1 over); SPI = EV / PV (>1 ahead, 1 on, <1 behind); EAC = BAC / CPI if CPI expected to continue; EAC = AC + BAC - EV if future work at planned rate; EAC = AC + bottom-up ETC if initial plan no longer valid; EAC = AC + [(BAC - EV)/(CPI x SPI)] if both indices influence remaining work; ETC = EAC - AC assuming work proceeds on plan, or ETC = reestimate from the bottom up; TCPI = (BAC - EV)/(BAC - AC) efficiency to complete on plan; TCPI = (BAC - EV)/(EAC - AC) efficiency to complete the current EAC; TCPI >1 harder to complete, 1 same, <1 easier. Source note: the Table 7-1 'How Used' text for SPI repeats cost wording ('how much costs are over or under the budgeted amount for work planned') - lessons describe SPI in schedule terms and flag this. PMIS monitors PV, EV, AC, shows trends and forecasts ranges. Outputs: WPI (work and cost variances at work package and control account level; CV, CPI, EAC, VAC, TCPI for work performance reports); cost forecasts (calculated or bottom-up EAC documented and communicated); change requests; plan updates (cost management plan - thresholds, accuracy; cost baseline; performance measurement baseline - revised when variances are severe); document updates (assumption log - productivity assumptions, basis of estimates, cost estimates - actual efficiency, lessons learned, risk register - when variances cross or may cross the cost threshold).

q-quality-overview.title: Project Quality Management overview: three processes, interrelations, quality vs grade, prevention vs inspection, COQ, five levels, trends
q-quality-overview.section: 8 intro, key concepts, trends, tailoring, agile (Figures 8-1, 8-2)
q-quality-overview.notes: Incorporate the organisation's quality policy for planning, managing and controlling project and product quality requirements to meet stakeholders' objectives; also supports continuous process improvement. Processes: 8.1 Plan Quality Management (identify quality requirements/standards and document how compliance will be demonstrated); 8.2 Manage Quality (translate the quality management plan into executable quality activities incorporating organisational quality policies); 8.3 Control Quality (monitor and record results of quality activities to assess performance and ensure outputs are complete, correct and meet customer expectations). Plan = the quality the work needs to have; Manage = managing the quality processes throughout; quality requirements become test and evaluation instruments in Manage Quality, applied in Control Quality to verify requirements; Control = compare results with requirements so the result is acceptable. Two outputs used by other areas: verified deliverables and quality reports. Figure 8-2 (verified): Plan Quality Management sends the quality management plan and quality metrics to Manage Quality; OPA quality templates also feed Manage Quality; Integration supplies deliverables and work performance data to Control Quality; Manage Quality sends test and evaluation documents and quality reports to Control Quality and quality reports to other processes; Control Quality returns quality control measurements and work performance information to Manage Quality, and sends verified deliverables to Validate Scope. Key concepts: applies to all projects; measures are deliverable-specific (software vs nuclear plant); failure has consequences (overworking the team, rushing inspections). Quality = 'the degree to which a set of inherent characteristics fulfill requirements' (ISO 9000, as quoted in the Guide); grade = a category for deliverables with the same functional use but different technical characteristics. Low quality is always a problem; low grade may not be (a low-grade, high-quality product may suit its purpose; a high-grade, low-quality product is a problem). The PM manages quality/grade trade-offs. Prevention is preferred over inspection - design quality in; preventing mistakes costs less than correcting them. Pairs to know: prevention (keep errors out of the process) vs inspection (keep errors out of the customer's hands); attribute sampling (conforms or not) vs variable sampling (continuous scale of conformity); tolerances (specified range of acceptable results) vs control limits (boundaries of common variation in a statistically stable process). Cost of quality (COQ): all costs over the product life for preventing nonconformance, appraising conformance and failing requirements (rework); failure costs are internal (found by the team) or external (found by the customer), a.k.a. cost of poor quality; life-cycle COQ decisions often belong to program/portfolio management, the PMO or operations. Five levels of increasingly effective quality management: let the customer find defects (most expensive: warranty, recalls, reputation, rework); detect and correct before delivery via quality control (appraisal and internal failure costs); quality assurance to correct the process itself; build quality into planning and design; create an organisation-wide culture committed to quality. Trends: customer satisfaction (conformance to requirements plus fitness for use; agile stakeholder engagement); continual improvement (PDCA cycle - Shewhart, modified by Deming; TQM, Six Sigma, Lean Six Sigma); management responsibility (all team members participate; management provides suitable resources at adequate capacity); mutually beneficial partnership with suppliers (long-term cooperative relationships over short-term gains). Tailoring: policy compliance and auditing, standards and regulatory compliance, continuous improvement level, stakeholder engagement. Agile: frequent quality and review steps throughout rather than at the end; recurring retrospectives check quality process effectiveness, find root causes and trial new approaches, later keeping, adjusting or dropping them; small batches uncover inconsistencies early when change is cheaper. q-8.1-plan-quality.title: 8.1 Plan Quality Management: COQ categories, cost-benefit, data representation, test and inspection planning, quality plan and metrics
q-8.1-plan-quality.notes: Identify quality requirements and/or standards for the project and deliverables and document how compliance will be demonstrated; key benefit: guidance on how quality will be managed and verified; once or at predefined points. Performed in parallel with other planning (quality changes may need cost/schedule adjustment and risk analysis). Inputs: charter (high-level description, product characteristics, approval requirements, measurable objectives, success criteria); plan (requirements management plan; risk management plan; stakeholder engagement plan; scope baseline - WBS and deliverables decide applicable standards and which deliverables/processes get quality review; acceptance criteria can significantly raise or lower quality costs; meeting all acceptance criteria implies stakeholder needs are met); documents (assumption log, requirements documentation incl. quality requirements, RTM - ensures each requirement is tested, overview of tests, risk register, stakeholder register - emphasis on customer and sponsor); EEFs (agency regulations, application-area rules and standards, geographic distribution, structure, marketplace, working/operating conditions, cultural perceptions); OPAs (organisational quality management system, quality templates such as check sheets and traceability matrices, historical databases and lessons learned). Tools: expert judgment (QA, QC, measurements, improvements, systems); data gathering - benchmarking (compare practices or standards with comparable projects, internal or external, same or other application areas), brainstorming, interviews (in an environment of trust and confidentiality); data analysis - cost-benefit analysis (is each quality activity cost-effective; benefits of meeting quality requirements: less rework, higher productivity, lower costs, more stakeholder satisfaction, higher profitability) and cost of quality: prevention costs (training, documenting processes, equipment, time to do it right), appraisal costs (testing, destructive testing loss, inspections) - together the cost of conformance, money spent during the project to avoid failures; internal failure costs (rework, scrap) and external failure costs (liabilities, warranty work, lost business) - cost of nonconformance, money spent during and after the project because of failures (Figure 8-5); optimal COQ balances prevention and appraisal against failure - beyond a point more prevention/appraisal is not cost-effective; decision making - multicriteria decision analysis/prioritisation matrix (weighted criteria scored across alternatives; here to prioritise quality metrics); data representation - flowcharts/process maps (sequence, decision points, loops, parallel paths; SIPOC = suppliers, inputs, process, outputs, customers with requirements and feedback loops - Figure 8-6; estimate COQ via branching logic and relative frequencies to compute expected monetary value of conformance and nonconformance work; identify where defects occur and where to add checks), logical data model (business-language view of data to find data integrity issues), matrix diagrams (strength of relationships between factors, causes, objectives; L, T, Y, X, C and roof-shaped; identify key quality metrics), mind mapping; test and inspection planning (how to test/inspect to meet needs and performance/reliability goals; industry dependent - alpha and beta tests in software, strength tests in construction, inspection in manufacturing, field and nondestructive tests in engineering); meetings. Outputs: quality management plan (how policies, procedures and guidelines will be implemented to meet quality objectives; reviewed early for value focus, lower cost, fewer rework overruns; contains quality standards, objectives, roles and responsibilities, deliverables and processes subject to review, QC and QM activities, tools, procedures for nonconformance, corrective action and continuous improvement); quality metrics (a specific project or product attribute and how Control Quality will verify compliance - e.g., % tasks on time, CPI, failure rate, defects per day, downtime per month, errors per line of code, customer satisfaction scores, % requirements covered by tests); plan updates (risk management plan, scope baseline incl. WBS dictionary quality requirements); document updates (lessons learned, RTM, risk register, stakeholder register). Data flow: charter from 4.1; outputs to plan and documents.
